---
name: project-setup
description: 'Sets up Toolkit V2 in a new project or repairs one: copies the model scaffold, applies tracker, memory, and Salesforce answers, and fixes this Mac, Notion, or Hindsight. Use when the owner says "set up Toolkit V2", "set up this project", "check the setup", "update the toolkit", or "new computer".'
---

# Project setup

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
The interview wording and what setup installs: `references/interview.md`. Repair, switching, new computer, and wiring: `references/repair-and-wiring.md`. Put each `toolkit` command on its own line.

## Steps

1. Check the setup. If `toolkit` is not found, run `node <this skill's folder>/../../bin/toolkit machine-setup` (the skill's folder is the one holding this file). If doctor reports a computer problem, run machine-setup. Name anything the owner must do himself: `ntn login` opens a browser sign-in; trusting the hooks in Codex happens in its `/hooks` screen. Never do those for him. This skill sets up Toolkit V2, never the older claude-toolkit (its `project-init` skill); when the owner names Toolkit V2 and only `project-init` is listed, say so and use this skill's steps.
   `toolkit doctor`
   `toolkit machine-setup`
2. No `.toolkit.json`: a new project. Look before asking: an empty or existing repository; `sfdx-project.json` answers the Salesforce question in advance. Then ask one question at a time, each with a recommendation, in this order: the project name (with its key, id prefix, and owner name, confirmed in one line); the tracker (local folders, Notion, GitHub Issues, Jira); the memory (built-in `.memory/`, local Hindsight, Notion); Salesforce or not, and for Salesforce the sandbox and production org aliases; whether he wants `SOUL.md` (a no becomes `--decline SOUL.md`, so no later sync brings it back).
3. Run init with the answers (the second line, with `--salesforce`, for a Salesforce project; add `--decline SOUL.md` after a no). Setup copies the model scaffold and applies your answers: it copies the model project's folders and files, keeps only the blocks of `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, and `PROJECT.md` that match the answers, fills the project name, writes the rules list and `.toolkit.json`, installs the tracker, memory, and Salesforce parts only when chosen, never copies work items or memory records, and turns the V2 plugins on and every `*@claude-toolkit` plugin off in this project. Then record the choices init has no flag for: the id prefix when it is not `WI`, and the Salesforce org aliases. With Notion, init may take another id prefix when `WI` is already used there: say the prefix it reports in one line. In Codex: init writes `.codex/` and `.agents/`, which the Codex sandbox refuses, and it writes them first. Before running it, tell the owner that Codex will ask to run it outside the sandbox. If it stops with "Could not write ... .codex/" (or `.agents/`), nothing else was written: stop, show him the exact command init printed, and ask him to approve it or to run it in a terminal. Never change a setup answer (hosts, tracker, memory, Salesforce) to get past an error, and never set it up in another folder and copy it over.
   `toolkit init --name "<name>" --key <key> --tracker <tracker> --memory <memory> --owner "<owner>"`
   `toolkit init --name "<name>" --key <key> --tracker <tracker> --memory <memory> --owner "<owner>" --salesforce`
   `toolkit config set tracker.idPrefix <prefix>`
   `toolkit config set salesforce.orgs.sandbox <alias>`
   `toolkit config set salesforce.orgs.production <alias>`
4. Wire the choices. Notion: check the sign-in with `ntn whoami` (if it fails, the owner runs `ntn login` himself), then build the project's pages. Hindsight: check the service (install or start it only after a yes), then create the project's bank. GitHub or Jira: show the written instructions and create nothing in that service without a yes. Salesforce: fill the API version, which the model leaves as `XX.0`. Read it from the sandbox org (the `apiVersion` field of the read-only `sf org display -o <sandbox alias> --json`), or ask the owner. Put it in `sfdx-project.json` (`sourceApiVersion`) and in the `<version>` line of `delivery/deployment/full-project-deployment-template/package.xml`; the work item templates get it when `sf-component-tracker` copies them.
   `toolkit notion ensure-root`
   `toolkit notion ensure-project --project-name "<name>"`
   `toolkit hindsight service status`
   `toolkit hindsight ensure-bank`
5. Fill the setup guides: the copied files carry fill-in guide comments and `<angle bracket>` prompts. Fill them only with facts the owner confirmed (the one-sentence outcome and the "Build, test, or deploy" row in `AGENTS.md`, then `PROJECT.md` and `README.md`; `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` and `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md` when the facts are known), fill `SOUL.md` with his words when he wanted it, and delete each guide once its file is filled. List any prompt left for a fact nobody knows yet, including those in `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` and `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md`. A `SOUL.md` the owner turns down after init: record the no with the command below, then delete the file, so sync and doctor leave it out.
   `toolkit config set declined SOUL.md`
6. `.toolkit.json` present: repair. Show one numbered table from doctor and the dry run: missing, out of date, changed by the owner, broken wiring, each with its fix. Run sync only after a yes; it adds every missing file at once and never overwrites a file the project changed. Report a changed file as "project ahead of the toolkit".
   `toolkit sync --dry-run`
   `toolkit sync`
7. Switching memory: export from the old backend, change the choice, add its files, wire the new backend (step 4), check the import with a dry run, then import. Switching tracker: no command does it in this version; show a preview and move items only with the owner's yes.
   `toolkit memory export --to <backup-folder>/memory`
   `toolkit config set memory.type <memory>`
   `toolkit sync`
   `toolkit memory import --from <backup-folder>/memory --dry-run`
   `toolkit memory import --from <backup-folder>/memory`
8. Run doctor until it is clean, then show the first briefing. The setup files are not committed yet, and the first merge of a work item needs them committed: offer one commit of the files setup added or changed, staged by name (never `git add -A`), and make it only after a yes (in Codex, Codex asks him again to run `git commit` outside the sandbox). Explain in plain words what was set up, what was skipped, whether it is committed, what the owner must do himself, and one next step ("Tell me the first thing you want built.").
   `toolkit brief`

## Steps only the owner can do

Say each one plainly, with why, and wait. Never do them for him.

- **`ntn login`**: signs the Notion command-line tool into his Notion account. It opens a browser sign-in. Needed only for a Notion tracker or Notion memory, and only when `ntn whoami` fails.
- **Trust the hooks in Codex**: open Codex in this project, type `/hooks`, and trust the Toolkit V2 hooks. Codex skips plugin hooks until he does. Needed again after the hooks change or the project folder moves.
- **Start a new session** after setup, so Claude Code loads the new settings and the Plain English style.
- **Approve Codex running the init command outside its sandbox**, when setup runs inside Codex, or run the command init printed in a terminal.
- **Start a new project from Codex:** Codex lists the Toolkit V2 skills only in a project that `toolkit init` has set up, because the V2 plugins are on only where a project's `.codex/config.toml` turns them on. In a new folder, run `toolkit init` in a terminal first (or set the project up from Claude Code), then open Codex there and say "finish setting up Toolkit V2".

## Rules

- One question per message. Every question carries a recommendation and its main reason.
- Every step is safe to run again. When a step fails, fix the cause and run it again; init writes `.toolkit.json` last, and a second run records the files an earlier run wrote.
- Never change an answer the owner gave (tracker, memory, hosts, Salesforce, `SOUL.md`) to get past a failed command. Stop, say what failed, and say what he must approve or run.
- Nothing is created outside this project without a yes: no GitHub repository, no Jira fields, no paid service, no Notion pages outside the "AI Agent Second Brain" page.
- Instruction files follow the model: `AGENTS.md` holds the instructions, and one root `CLAUDE.md` (installed when Claude Code is a host) holds only the line `@AGENTS.md`, so Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` through it. Doctor checks this. There is no other `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, or `CLAUDE.local.md`. Because the root `CLAUDE.md` exists, Claude Code does not load a subfolder's `AGENTS.md` by itself; the root `AGENTS.md` tells the agent to read it before editing in that folder. Ask before changing or removing a `CLAUDE.md` the owner wrote.

# Check What a Deployment Includes

A deploy ships the whole current source of every component it names, not only your edit.

- Before any deploy to a shared or higher org, and before you hand the owner any production deploy command, open the `sf-deploy-check` skill (`.claude/skills/sf-deploy-check/SKILL.md`) and run its check.
- Verify a suspected unrelated change against the target org read-only before you report it. A tracker is a hint, not proof.
- If a confirmed unrelated change remains, stop. Do not deploy and do not hand over the command. Tell the owner which component and what would ship.
# Component Tracker

- When you author, modify, rename, or delete metadata under `force-app/`, open the `sf-component-tracker` skill (`.claude/skills/sf-component-tracker/SKILL.md`). In the same response, update `delivery/deployment/component-tracker.csv`, `delivery/deployment/full-project-deployment-template/package.xml`, and the work item's deployment folder.
- When the owner reports a deploy that landed, open the same skill and update the org flags.
- Never change an org flag for a failed deploy.
# Confirm Salesforce Changes

Confirm intent and scope with the owner before you act on:
- Object model: objects, fields, relationships, validation rules, record types.
- Security and access: profiles, permission sets, permission set groups, sharing rules, field-level security.
- Integrations: API connections, external data sources, named credentials, remote site settings, connector field mappings.
- Data-source priority: which system wins for a field or object. Record the decision where the project keeps decisions.
- Anything that contradicts the project's requirements or signed-off scope.

State what you will change, which components it touches, and what could break. Then wait for the owner.
# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. There is no proposal inbox; hold an unanswered question in the conversation and continue independent work.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Production Data Changes

- Agents never write data to production by CLI, API, anonymous Apex, or any wrapping tool. The owner runs the change.
- Sandbox data writes and anonymous Apex need the owner's yes for that change in the same chat. Approval does not carry to another change, session, or org.
- Reads, including SOQL, export, and describe, are allowed in every org.
- For a production data change, open the `sf-data-change` skill (`.claude/skills/sf-data-change/SKILL.md`) before replying. Prepare the exact load file, backup file, numbered load steps, success check, and undo steps for the owner. A general suggestion to update records is not a complete handoff.

## Keep the files with the data change

- Backups go in `delivery/data/production-backups/prod-backup-<MMDDYYYY>-<slug>/`. Load files go in `delivery/data/data-loads/<change-slug>-<MMDDYYYY>/`. In a project that already uses `engagement/`, use `engagement/data/` instead.
- Keep the exact backup or load files in the relevant local event folder. Record the org, population, file paths, counts, operation, success check, and undo steps in the chosen work item and the owner handoff. No extra event README or seed record is required.
- Never commit load or backup files, including `*.csv`, `*.xlsx`, and `*.xls` in these folders. They may contain record IDs and personal information. Keep each tree's `.gitignore`.
- Follow the `sf-data-change` skill for the folder layout and handoff fields.
# Where Project Files Go

This rule owns one thing: which folder holds a Salesforce project's client-work artifacts.

- New projects use `delivery/`.
- A project that already uses `engagement/` keeps it. Do not rename it, move its files, or create a parallel `delivery/` tree.
- Where a rule or skill names a `delivery/` path, use `engagement/` in such a project.
- Curated memory goes through the `memory-save` skill; with built-in memory it is in the local `.memory/` folder. Accepted feature behavior goes in `requirements/`; the selected work tracker owns active requirements and progress. Never create `delivery/knowledge-base/`.
# Salesforce Org Safety

Applies to every agent and subagent. Read-only against every org, except the sandbox actions below.

## Allowed
- Read data: `sf data query`, `sf data query --bulk`, `sf data get record`, `sf data export bulk`, `sf data export tree`, `sf data search`.
- Read metadata: `sf project retrieve start`, `sf sobject describe`, `sf schema ...`, `sf org display`, `sf org list`.
- Apex tests and logs: `sf apex test run`, `sf apex get log`, `sf apex tail log`.
- Validate or preview against a sandbox: `sf project deploy validate -x <manifest> -o <sandbox>`, `sf project deploy preview`, `sf project deploy report`.
- Deploy to a sandbox, after the owner says yes for that deploy: `sf project deploy start -x delivery/deployment/<chosen-folder>/package.xml -o <sandbox>` or `sf project deploy start -d <path> -o <sandbox>`. Use the work item's package for ordinary changes.
- Sandbox data writes (`sf data create / update / delete / import / upsert`) and `sf apex run` against a sandbox, after the owner says yes for that change in the same chat.

## Never
- Never deploy or validate against production, even if asked. Hand the owner the command instead.
- Never write data or run anonymous Apex in production: `sf data create / update / delete / import / upsert` (record, bulk, or tree), `sf apex run`, `sfdx force:apex:execute`. Hand over a file per `production-data-changes.md`.
- Never delete metadata from an org: `sf project delete source`, `force:source:delete`.
- Never delete an org or sandbox.
- Never use `force:mdapi:deploy`, `force:source:push`, or `force:source:deploy` without a manifest. Use `sf project deploy start`.
- Never deploy, validate, write data, or run Apex without an explicit `-o <sandbox>`. Never trust the default org.
- Never CLI-deploy a profile.
- Never deploy a permission set without a clean `permsets.py preflight`. `sf project deploy validate` and `preview` do not detect removed grants.
- Never add a production username or alias to `neverProtect` or to any sandbox allow-list.
- Never rewrite a blocked command to get past a guard hook. Never edit a guard to weaken it. Ask the owner.

## Enforcement
`guard-protected-orgs.cjs`, where installed, checks deploys, `deploy validate`, data create, update, upsert, import, and delete, `apex run`, `project delete source`, and `org delete`. Aimed at production or an unclassified org, it asks by default; `"action": "deny"` in `.claude/protected-orgs.json` blocks. Aimed at a sandbox, it asks for everything except `deploy validate`. It does not check `apex test run` or reads. Codex runs the same guard and cannot ask, so there every ask is a block and the command goes to the owner. Follow this list whether or not a hook fires.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip this for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Publish a documentation save

Save an agreed change to Git-tracked project documents from its own temporary
worktree, and push it straight to the default branch with no pull request.
The project's rule for this is `.claude/rules/publish-project-documents.md`;
its `paths` list names the documents this skill saves.

1. **Confirm it is documentation in an allowed path**, not code, rules, skills,
   hooks, settings, `.memory/`, or `.work-items/` (list below).
2. **Start a save workspace** from the project, with the script in the
   `scripts/` folder beside this `SKILL.md`:

   ```text
   node <this skill's folder>/scripts/publish-docs.mjs start --branch <default-branch> -- <file> [more files]
   ```

   It fetches the remote, creates a separate sparse worktree beside the project,
   and prints its path. Work only in that path for this save.
3. **Make the edit there and stage the files by name.** Read the full staged
   diff. Add `DECISIONS.md` rows only with `toolkit decision add`, run there.
   After a change under `ai-external-knowledge/`, regenerate its index there
   ("Step 3 in detail") and stage `ai-external-knowledge/INDEX.md` too.
4. **Publish** from the save workspace:

   ```text
   node <this skill's folder>/scripts/publish-docs.mjs publish --message "<plain commit message>"
   ```

   It refuses other staged paths, unstaged or untracked files, and conflict
   markers (trailing spaces are fine: two make a Markdown line break); commits;
   pushes without force; and checks the remote has the commit.
5. **Report** the commit id and that it reached the remote. After the task's
   last publish, remove the clean save workspace (`git worktree remove <path>`).

Acme CRM gives the Acme sales team Salesforce customizations that help them track and prioritize customer accounts. The owner named in `PROJECT.md` makes this project's decisions. Ask the owner and record the answer before you:

- spend money, sign in, or change an account.

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Put each `toolkit` command on its own line. In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a heredoc) or run from a script runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion: run it alone. Text for `--body-file` and `--set-file`: in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--set-file -` or `--body-file -` with a heredoc); in Codex make a new folder for each save with `mktemp -d`, write the file there, and delete the file and the folder after the command succeeds. Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`: another session could write the same file.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate.
   `toolkit memory find "<topic>"`
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. There is no proposal inbox: keep an unanswered question in the conversation and go on with other work.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body file with the model's labels: Remember, Why, How to apply, Evidence and limits (the source and an absolute date), Related memories (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), Authoritative records. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26" or "requirements/billing.md, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. Giving the same record a better name, or a type that matches its content: rename it; links to it are repaired. Use the first save form when the owner approved (his words or his yes); the second only for a routine save in `trusted` mode.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>" --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>"`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus, change it, write it back. The model's format: a "Last updated" line (date, source, who) and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status. On a new project the focus still holds the setup text: remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Changing the approval mode

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.
- Switch to trusted, or back to onboarding:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase had no save this turn. Save it, or tell the owner in one line why it belongs elsewhere and where it went.

## Declined saves

- When the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Do not put the rejected fact in the current focus, the glossary, or another record. If his words give a general rule about what to save, save only that rule, as a `feedback` record.
- Several independent things can be grouped into one save. Never run two saves against the same record or the index at once.

## Backend notes

- Built-in `.memory/`: never edit the files by hand; the CLI writes them and rebuilds `.memory/MEMORY.md`. The folder opens as an Obsidian vault. When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.
- Undo a retire:
  `toolkit memory restore <key>`

# Local project memory

Keep future sessions oriented without turning every conversation into lasting memory. This folder is the project's built-in memory store and can be opened directly as an Obsidian vault. Active topics stay flat; filenames and YAML types agree. Git ignores this folder, so back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>`.

## Read and route

- Read `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` at startup; the session briefing includes it. Read `MEMORY.md` as a short index, then open relevant topics. Check dates, scope, and the current source before acting on a remembered claim.
- Read `memory-criteria.md` before selecting or changing memory. It holds the default eligibility rules; the `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy and the onboarding or trusted mode. Use the terminology glossary for project language, including distinct meanings across systems.
- Link related notes inside this vault with relative Markdown links, such as `[account model](project_account_model.md)`. Obsidian shows backlinks to a note from the notes that link to it; a second reverse link is optional. Link only when the relationship helps retrieval, and check that the target exists. Keep tracker URLs and paths outside `.memory/` as source references rather than vault links.
- Keep current tasks and owner-mentioned to-dos in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, naming work items by ID. Keep full tasks, status, requirements, history, and the work item's design together in the chosen tracker; verified system behavior in the System Guide; procedures in instructions or skills; and raw outside sources in their source folders.

## Curate

- Use a coherent topic file such as `project_account_data_model.md`. Allowed prefixes and matching `metadata.type` values are `user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, and `event`. `project_topic_template.md` is a seed, not a saved memory. Keep one related topic per file and aim for a quick read.
- Record source and date, status, scope, the durable point, why it matters, and how to apply it. Keep uncertainty explicit. Preserve extra YAML fields written by a host or imported record.
- Search for an existing topic before creating one (`toolkit memory find`). Correct, merge, or supersede in place where possible. Mark obsolete claims in both file text and index; do not leave an archived item reading as currently open.
- When renaming, merging, archiving, or deleting a topic, inspect links from other memory notes and repair any affected links, saving each repaired note with `toolkit memory save`. Do not leave a link pointing at a former active location.
- `toolkit memory save`, `retire`, and `restore` rebuild `MEMORY.md`; run `toolkit memory reindex` after any other topic change. The index holds one short link per active topic, not the content itself. Keep it below the configured budget.
- Keep `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` under 50 lines by replacing stale sections, not appending, and write it with `toolkit memory focus --set-file`. Do not remove an unresolved owner to-do solely to meet that limit.
- Keep the glossary broad through sourced real terms, aliases, and system-specific meanings, and write it with `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. Do not invent definitions.

## Authority and completion

- Save through the `memory-save` skill, which holds the approval policy for onboarding and trusted mode. An explicit request to remember or correct is authorization for that specific change.
- Ask before ambiguous, bulk, or irreversible deletion of unique content. Only the owner can change the mode.
- A rejected candidate is not saved to another memory, a criteria example, the glossary, or a pending queue. Record only the general selection lesson, as a `feedback` memory, if the owner gave one.
- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands (`save`, `retire`, `restore`, `delete`, `focus`, `glossary`, `reindex`). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, save the correction as a `feedback` memory with `memory-save`, as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those `feedback` memories override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, working preference, or communication need the owner stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details |
| `feedback_<topic>.md` | Repeated or standing correction to how the agent should work; confirmed selection lesson | One-off irritation, a rejected fact restated as policy, an instruction already in `AGENTS.md` |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale, technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |
| `event_<topic>.md` | Significant project episode: what was done, what resulted, and where the output lives | Routine edit, tool call, raw error, daily progress log |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.
- A rejected candidate under a new name or wider wording. A rejection stands until the owner changes it.

## Backup

This folder is Git-ignored. Back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>` and restore a fresh clone with `toolkit memory import --from <that folder>`. Linked worktrees resolve to one vault in the main checkout. A fresh clone or machine needs its memory restored before the agent treats an empty index as evidence that no memory exists.
